claims.feature: other: universalising by detaching from a named context
claims.claim: Kay claims that setting a story as fantasy detaches the tale from a narrow context.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Home and Away', BrightWeavings
claims.quote: It detaches the tale from a narrow context
claims.page: body, 'what can fantasy do better' section

claims.feature: other: honesty about the limits of historical knowledge
claims.claim: Kay argues that treating the past as fantasy is a way of being honest about limitations.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Home and Away', BrightWeavings
claims.quote: a way of being honest about limitations

claims.feature: other: escape that returns the reader home
claims.claim: Kay endorses Douglas Barbour's description of admired fantasy as the kind of escape that brings you home; the phrase is Barbour's, quoted by Kay.
claims.source: Douglas Barbour, quoted approvingly by Guy Gavriel Kay in 'Home and Away', BrightWeavings
claims.quote: The kind of escape that brings you home.

claims.feature: other: competing versions of one story
claims.claim: Kay asserts that all renderings of a legend matter and that the changes between versions carry truths about the societies that made them.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'On Myth' (Chapters 'Great Writers' series newspaper insert)

claims.claim: Kay states that in the study of myth the earliest version of a legend is not always the most important.
claims.quote: the earliest version of a legend isn’t always the

claims.claim: Kay says he tried to write Tigana's themes in with a stiletto rather than a bludgeon, slipping them in quietly while keeping the reader turning pages.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, Afterword to the ROC USA tenth anniversary edition of Tigana, reprinted on BrightWeavings
claims.quote: I tried to imagine myself with a stiletto not a bludgeon

claims.claim: Kay says he wanted to open a book about subterfuge and deception with an outright lie, and that the first sentence of chapter one does so.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, Tigana Afterword (1999), BrightWeavings
claims.quote: start a book about subterfuge and deception with an outright lie
claims.page: paragraph on first sentence and music

claims.claim: Kay says the two Prague Spring photographs showed a functionary not only killed but made never to have been, and that this image lingered twenty years and seeded Tigana.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, Tigana Afterword (1999), BrightWeavings
claims.quote: not only killed, but made to never have been

claims.claim: Kay states that names link to history and that a sense of history is needed to define ourselves.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, Tigana Afterword (1999), BrightWeavings

claims.claim: Kay rejects the idea that fantasy is essentially about variations on hyphens and apostrophes in invented names.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'On Writing Sailing to Sarantium', written for Earthlight (UK publisher)
claims.quote: hyphens and apostrophes in invented names
claims.page: middle section on what fantasy is

claims.claim: Kay says he is happy establishing a space between the invented character and the real man on whom he is based.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, Under Heaven Author's Letter, printed in the advance reading copies
claims.quote: a space between the invented character and the real man
claims.page: paragraph on the Tang prime minister

claims.claim: Kay says the shift from real China to an imagined Kitai serves notice that he reserves the right to change or telescope events.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, Under Heaven Author's Letter (2010)
claims.quote: I reserve the right to change, or telescope events
claims.page: paragraph on keeping readers turning pages

claims.feature: other: accumulated detail as reader trust
claims.claim: Kay claims the quiet, steady accumulation of detail and complexity reaches readers almost subliminally and earns their trust in the book.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Rodger Turner for SFSite
claims.quote: the quiet, steady accumulation of detail
claims.page: answer on the 'credibility of the book'

claims.claim: Kay says what we know of the great figures of the past is shaped by, and at the mercy of, those who chronicled them, citing Procopius on Justinian and Theodora.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Rodger Turner for SFSite
claims.quote: at the mercy of!) those who chronicled them

claims.claim: Kay says a viewpoint character observing a setting for the first time serves as a window for the reader, so the character's initiation becomes the reader's.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Rodger Turner for SFSite
claims.quote: A viewpoint character who is observing a setting for the first
claims.page: answer on the 'fish out of water' technique
